proposals.impact: restores daily content pipeline blocked since 08:57 yesterday
proposals.observation: Three CI workflows failed on 21 September: Daily Blog Post (08:57), Weekly Monday Report (11:07), and Funnel-Hack Digest (15:20). No commits landed in the last 24 hours. The content queue sits at one remaining post. If that single queued post publishes before the workflow is repaired, the blog goes dark with no automated recovery. This is the highest-urgency item in the data because it silences every downstream channel that depends on fresh content.
proposals.proposal: Diagnose and patch the Daily Blog Post workflow. The three failures in ascending time order suggest a shared dependency broke around 09:00 on 21 September — likely an API key rotation, a changed secret name, or a dependency version bump that landed in the environment without a corresponding commit. Open the workflow run log for the 08:57 failure first. Identify the first non-zero exit line. That line is the fix target. Do not touch astro.config.mjs or .github/workflows files that are outside the Daily Blog Post workflow — the blocked-paths list covers all workflow files, so the repair must be made in the workflow's configuration inputs (environment secrets, caller parameters) rather than the workflow YAML itself. If the secret has rotated, update it in the GitHub repo settings under Actions secrets, which is not a file edit and therefore outside the blocked-path scope.

proposals.impact: closes 29-point open-rate gap between Money Worship and Money Vigilance sequences
proposals.observation: Money Vigilance emails: 12 sent, 66.67% open rate. Money Worship emails: 16 sent, 37.5% open rate. That is a 29-percentage-point gap between two sequences of similar size. The sequences run on the same platform, to a list built from the same quiz. The most likely explanation is the subject line for Money Worship email 1 is generic enough that recipients do not recognise themselves in it. Money Vigilance subscribers open at two-thirds — which suggests that subject line names a felt experience precisely. Money Worship subscribers are opening at roughly the rate of a cold list. Fixing the subject line is a one-line change with no structural risk.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the Money Worship sequence email-1 subject line so it names a specific, felt behaviour rather than a category label. The current line almost certainly uses the phrase "money worship" or a close synonym, which reads as a clinical tag rather than a mirror. The replacement should reflect what a Money Worship scorer actually does on a Tuesday evening, not what a taxonomy calls them. Joel's ICP for this segment: earns well, ties self-worth to the next income number, feels uneasy when not earning, avoids looking at what the money is actually for. The new subject line should make that person feel seen before they open the email.

proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I check my balance at midnight then close the tab before the number loads?"
pubDate: "2026-09-23"
description: "The tab opens. The spinner spins. You close it. That sequence is not laziness or forgetfulness — it is a decision your nervous system makes on your behalf, and it is worth looking at honestly."
tags: ["money avoidance", "behavioural money", "quiet awareness"]
---

You know the move. It is late. You open the banking app or the spreadsheet or the HMRC login you have been meaning to check for three weeks. The page starts to load. You close it.

Not because you got distracted. Because some part of you decided, in the half-second before the number appeared, that tonight is not the night to know.

That is not a character flaw. It is information.

Joel works with people who earn well and still do this. Salaries that would have floored their twenty-two-year-old selves. Invoices going out, money coming in. And still, the tab closes before the number lands.

The pattern usually runs like this: if the number is good, looking at it feels like tempting fate. If the number is bad, looking at it means having to do something about it. Either way, not-knowing feels safer than knowing. So the tab closes. The decision gets deferred. The account stays open in another window, loaded but unread, like a letter pushed to the back of the kitchen drawer.

This is what behavioural economists call strategic ignorance. It is not random avoidance. It is a choice your brain makes because certainty carries cost and uncertainty, at least in the short term, carries none.

The problem is that the cost of not-knowing compounds. Not in a dramatic way. In the ordinary way of a tax return you genuinely forgot about until February, or a pension you set up in 2021 and have not logged into since, or a direct debit that cleared last month and you cannot quite remember what it was for.

None of those things are emergencies. That is exactly why they stay undone.

If you recognise the midnight-tab pattern in yourself, the useful question is not "why am I so bad with money?" That question assumes the answer is about discipline, and it is not. The useful question is: what are you protecting yourself from knowing?

Sometimes the answer is a number that confirms a fear you have held quietly for years. Sometimes it is evidence that the money is fine, which is almost worse, because then you have to ask what you have been so afraid of.

Joel's MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner background sits underneath all of this, but the conversation he actually has with clients is not about the number. It is about what the number means to them, and why they have been managing their relationship with that meaning by not looking.

The tab will load eventually. It always does.

The question is whether you want to be the one deciding when, or whether you want to keep leaving that to midnight and a closed browser.

If you want to understand the pattern underneath your own money behaviour, the quiz on this site takes about four minutes and names it precisely. No optimism. No action plan you will abandon by Thursday. Just an honest reckoning with the story beneath the number.
